title: Keeping the Program in Memory
objective: After this level you can explain why storing the program in memory beside its data, first done in 1948, made computers flexible.
summary: A stored-program computer keeps instructions in memory beside its data, proposed in 1945, so a program changes without rewiring. The Manchester Baby first did it on June 21, 1948.

cards.headline: What if changing a program meant changing numbers, not cables?
cards.body: Setting ENIAC up for each problem took many days of wiring and switch setting. The fix sounds almost too simple: keep the instructions in the computer's memory, right beside the data they work on.

cards.headline: Instructions are data too
cards.body: In a stored-program computer, instructions and data sit together in the same memory. John von Neumann and colleagues proposed the design in 1945, for a machine called EDVAC. Because a program is just more data in memory, it can be changed, moved or even produced by another program, with no rewiring at all.

mascot.line: This is Level 13's universal machine made real: the program is just more data for the machine to read.

cards.fact: On June 21, 1948, the Manchester Baby ran a program stored in its memory.
cards.context: It was the first computer to do so. Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill built it at the University of Manchester. Its memory was a Williams-Kilburn tube, which stored bits on a cathode-ray tube. Its first program searched for the highest factor of a number, not glamorous, but it worked.

cards.headline: The birth of software
cards.body: The Computer History Museum calls this moment the birth of software: storing a computer's instructions in its memory, as every computer since has done. A new job now meant loading new instructions, not days with cables and switches.
